notes.title: Light Propagation, Speed & Snell's Law
content: Light travels in straight ray paths within a homogeneous optical medium (Ray Approximation Model).[cite: 2]
The Law of Reflection states that the incident ray, reflected ray, and normal lie in the same plane, with θi = θr measured strictly from the surface normal.[cite: 2]
Refractive index (n) represents the factor by which the phase velocity of light is reduced in a medium (n = c / v >= 1.00).[cite: 2]
Snell's Law governs wave bending at planar interfaces: n_a sin(θ_a) = n_b sin(θ_b). When moving to a denser medium (n_b > n_a), rays bend TOWARD the normal (θ_b < θ_a).[cite: 2]
Wave frequency (f) remains invariant across media boundaries, while wavelength shrinks in denser media (λ = λ₀ / n).[cite: 2]

notes.title: Total Internal Reflection & Fiber Optics
content: Total Internal Reflection (TIR) occurs exclusively when light propagates from an optically denser medium to a less dense medium (n_a > n_b).[cite: 2]
At the critical angle (θ_crit), the refracted ray emerges at 90° along the boundary surface: sin(θ_crit) = n_b / n_a.[cite: 2]
If the angle of incidence exceeds θ_crit, no light refracts into the second medium and 100% of the wave energy is reflected back.[cite: 2]
Porro Prisms (45°-45°-90°) utilize TIR at 45° (since glass-air θ_crit ≈ 41.1°) to invert image rays in binoculars without reflection losses.[cite: 2]
Optical Fibers transmit signals via core TIR. The Numerical Aperture (NA = sin θ_i = √(n_core² - n_clad²)) defines the acceptance cone angle for internal guiding.[cite: 2]

notes.title: Chromatic Dispersion & Prism Deviation
content: Chromatic Dispersion occurs because a material's refractive index varies inversely with wavelength n(λ).[cite: 2]
In normal dispersion, shorter wavelengths (violet, ~400 nm) experience a higher refractive index n and slower speed v than longer wavelengths (red, ~700 nm).[cite: 2]
When white light enters a prism, violet light undergoes the maximum deviation angle δ, separating white light into a rainbow spectrum.[cite: 2]
Minimum Deviation (δ_min) occurs when light travels symmetrically through a prism with apex angle A (θ_a1 = θ_a2 and θ_b1 = θ_b2).[cite: 2]
Angular Dispersion Spread (Δδ = δ_violet - δ_red) quantifies the angular rainbow separation produced by a prism.[cite: 2]

notes.title: Exam Pitfalls: Refraction & Media Transitions
content: ALWAYS measure incidence and refraction angles from the normal (perpendicular axis), NOT the glass surface.[cite: 2]
When light passes through a slab with parallel boundaries, the emerging ray travels parallel to the original incident ray (θ_emerge = θ_incident).[cite: 2]
Do NOT change frequency f when calculating wave parameters in a new medium; only velocity v and wavelength λ change.[cite: 2]
TIR is mathematically IMPOSSIBLE if n_a < n_b (e.g., light traveling from air into glass cannot undergo TIR).[cite: 2]

notes.title: Electromagnetic Wave Properties & Intensity
content: Electromagnetic waves are transverse waves consisting of mutually perpendicular electric (E) and magnetic (B) fields oscillating in phase.[cite: 2]
The wave propagation speed in vacuum is governed by fundamental constants: c = 1 / √(ε₀ μ₀) ≈ 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s.[cite: 2]
Field magnitudes are strictly coupled by E_max = c B_max at every instant.[cite: 2]
The Poynting Vector S = (E × B) / μ₀ represents the directional instantaneous energy flux density in W/m².[cite: 2]
Wave Intensity (I) is the time-averaged magnitude of the Poynting vector: I = S_av = 1/2 ε₀ c E_max² = E_max² / (2 μ₀ c).[cite: 2]

notes.title: Polarization States & Superposition
content: Linear Polarization: E-field vector oscillates in a single fixed plane along the propagation path.[cite: 2]
Superposition of two orthogonal linearly polarized waves E_x and E_y with zero phase difference (Δφ = 0) yields a linearly polarized wave at angle θ = arctan(E_0y / E_0x).[cite: 2]
Circular Polarization: Formed by combining two orthogonal waves with equal amplitudes (E_0x = E_0y) and a phase difference of Δφ = ±π/2 (90°).[cite: 2]
Elliptical Polarization: Results when orthogonal waves have unequal amplitudes (E_0x ≠ E_0y) or arbitrary phase shifts (Δφ ≠ 0, π/2, π).[cite: 2]

notes.title: Polarizing Filters, Malus's Law & Brewster's Law
content: Unpolarized light passing through a single ideal polarizer loses 50% of its intensity, becoming linearly polarized: I_1 = 0.5 I_0.[cite: 2]
Polarized light passing through an analyzer follows Malus's Law: I = I_max cos²(φ), where φ is the relative angle between transmission axes.[cite: 2]

Polarization by Reflection: When unpolarized light strikes a flat surface at Brewster's Angle (θ_p), the reflected ray becomes 100% linearly polarized perpendicular to the plane of incidence.[cite: 2]
Brewster's Condition: Brewster's angle satisfies tan(θ_p) = n_b / n_a. At this exact angle, the reflected ray and refracted ray are mutually perpendicular (θ_p + θ_b = 90°).[cite: 2]

notes.title: Exam Tips: Multi-Polarizer Stacks
content: Two crossed polarizers at 90° block ALL light transmission (I = 0).[cite: 2]
Inserting a 3rd polarizer at an intermediate angle θ between two crossed 90° polarizers ALLOWS light to pass through! Calculate sequentially using Malus's Law.[cite: 2]
For a 3-filter stack where Filter 1 is at 0°, Filter 2 is at θ, and Filter 3 is at 90°: I_final = (1/2 I_0) * cos²(θ) * cos²(90° - θ) = 1/8 I_0 sin²(2θ).[cite: 2]
When glass is immersed in water (n = 1.33), Brewster's angle CHANGES because n_a is no longer 1.00: tan(θ_p) = n_glass / n_water.[cite: 2]

notes.title: Spherical Mirror Image Formation
content: Concave Mirrors (f > 0, R > 0) converge parallel rays to a real focal point in front of the mirror.[cite: 2]
Convex Mirrors (f < 0, R < 0) diverge parallel rays away from a virtual focal point behind the mirror.[cite: 2]
Paraxial Approximation assumes small ray angles α relative to the optic axis, focusing all rays to a single point f = R / 2.[cite: 2]
Spherical Aberration occurs for non-paraxial rays, smearing out point images.[cite: 2]
The Mirror Equation relates object distance s, image distance s', and focal length f: 1/s + 1/s' = 1/f = 2/R.[cite: 2]

notes.title: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces & Apparent Depth
content: Light refracting across a curved spherical boundary between media n_a and n_b forms an image according to: n_a/s + n_b/s' = (n_b - n_a)/R.[cite: 2]
Lateral magnification at a single spherical refracting boundary is given by: m = y'/y = -(n_a s') / (n_b s).[cite: 2]
Apparent Depth: For a flat surface (R -> ∞), the equation simplifies to n_a/s + n_b/s' = 0, giving s' = -(n_b / n_a) s.[cite: 2]
Looking straight down into a swimming pool (n_a = 1.33 water into n_b = 1.00 air), the water appears shallower by a factor of 3/4.[cite: 2]

notes.title: Thin Lenses & Lensmaker's Equation
content: A Thin Lens consists of two spherical refracting surfaces whose thickness is negligible compared to image distances.[cite: 2]
Lensmaker's Equation calculates focal length f from refractive index n and surface radii: 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R_1 - 1/R_2).[cite: 2]
Converging Lenses (f > 0, thicker in center) focus parallel incident rays to a real focal point behind the lens.[cite: 2]
Diverging Lenses (f < 0, thinner in center) bend parallel incident rays away from a virtual focal point in front of the lens.[cite: 2]
Optical Power (P) measures light-bending strength in Diopters (D = m⁻¹): P = 1 / f (in meters).[cite: 2]

notes.title: Master Sign Conventions (Mirrors & Lenses)
content: Object Distance s: Positive if object is on incoming light side (Real Object). Negative for Virtual Object.[cite: 2]
Image Distance s': Positive if image is on OUTGOING light side (Real Image). Negative if on incoming side (Virtual Image).[cite: 2]
Radius of Curvature R: Positive if center of curvature C is on OUTGOING light side. Negative if C is on incoming side.[cite: 2]
For Mirrors: Real images (s' > 0) are in FRONT of mirror. For Lenses: Real images (s' > 0) are BEHIND lens.[cite: 2]
Magnification m: Negative m = Inverted image. Positive m = Upright image. |m| > 1 = Enlarged, |m| < 1 = Diminished.[cite: 2]

notes.title: Young's Double-Slit Interference
content: Thomas Young's experiment proved the wave nature of light using two coherent monochromatic slit sources S1 and S2 separated by distance d.[cite: 2]
Path Difference Δr = d sin(θ) creates bright and dark interference bands on a distant screen at distance R (where R >> d).[cite: 2]
Constructive Interference (Bright Maxima): Waves arrive in phase when path difference is an integral multiple of wavelength: d sin(θ) = m λ (m = 0, ±1, ±2...).[cite: 2]
Destructive Interference (Dark Minima): Waves arrive 180° out of phase when path difference is a half-integral multiple: d sin(θ) = (m + 0.5) λ.[cite: 2]
Under small-angle approximation (tan θ ≈ sin θ ≈ y / R), fringe spacing Δy = λ R / d is constant across central screen regions.[cite: 2]

notes.title: Double-Slit Intensity & Phase Shift Distribution
content: Total Phase Difference φ between two overlapping waves: φ = (2π / λ) d sin(θ) = (2π d y) / (λ R).[cite: 2]
Interference Intensity Formula: I = I_0 cos²(φ / 2) = I_0 cos²[(π d y) / (λ R)].[cite: 2]
Peak Intensity I_0 represents the central maximum intensity, which is four times greater than the intensity from a single isolated slit (I_0 = 4 I_single).[cite: 2]
Energy Conservation: Energy is redistributed from dark minima (I = 0) to bright maxima (I = 4 I_single), preserving total spatial power.[cite: 2]
equations: I = I_0 \cos^2\left(\frac{\phi}{2}\right) = I_0 \cos^2\left(\frac{\pi d y}{\lambda R}\right)

notes.title: Thin-Film Interference & Reflection Phase Rules
content: Reflection Phase Shift Rule: An EM wave undergoing reflection at an interface experiences a half-cycle phase reversal (180° or π rad shift) ONLY IF reflecting off an optically denser medium (n_inc < n_refl).[cite: 2]
No phase reversal (0 rad shift) occurs when reflecting off a lower refractive index medium (n_inc > n_refl).[cite: 2]
Light travels an extra round-trip distance of 2t inside a film of thickness t and index n_film, where internal wavelength is contracted: λ_film = λ₀ / n_film.[cite: 2]
ONE Relative Phase Shift (e.g., Air [1.00] -> Oil [1.40] -> Water [1.33]): Constructive Reflection: 2 t n_film = (m + 0.5) λ₀. Destructive Reflection: 2 t n_film = m λ₀.[cite: 2]
ZERO or TWO Relative Phase Shifts (e.g., Air [1.00] -> Soap [1.33] -> Glass [1.52]): Constructive Reflection: 2 t n_film = m λ₀. Destructive Reflection: 2 t n_film = (m + 0.5) λ₀.[cite: 2]
equations: 2 t n_{\text{film}} = m \lambda_0 \quad (\text{0 or 2 shifts, bright})

notes.title: Newton's Rings & Michelson Interferometer
content: Newton's Rings: Formed by an air/liquid wedge film between a plano-convex lens (radius R) and a flat plate.[cite: 2]
The central contact point O is strictly DARK in reflection because path length is zero but top reflection undergoes a 180° phase shift.[cite: 2]
Radii of Newton's Dark Rings: r_m ≈ √(m λ₀ R / n_film).[cite: 2]
Michelson Interferometer uses a beam splitter to divide light along two perpendicular mirror paths (fixed M1, movable M2).[cite: 2]
Displacing mirror M2 by distance y causes a path change of 2y, moving m bright fringes across the viewing crosshairs: y = m λ₀ / 2.[cite: 2]

notes.title: Single-Slit Fraunhofer Diffraction
content: Diffraction is the bending of wave fronts around aperture obstacles, explained via Huygens's principle where every point on an open slit acts as a source of secondary wavelets.[cite: 2]
Fraunhofer Diffraction assumes parallel incident light and a distant observation screen (R >> a).[cite: 2]
Single-Slit Minima Condition: Dark fringes occur at angles satisfying a sin(θ) = m λ, where m = ±1, ±2, ±3... (m ≠ 0).[cite: 2]
The Central Bright Maximum is centered at m = 0 and is TWICE as wide as secondary side maxima.[cite: 2]
Total linear width of central bright maximum on screen: w = 2 y_1 = 2 R λ / a.[cite: 2]

notes.title: Single-Slit Intensity & Phasor Derivation
content: Dividing a single slit of width a into infinitely many strip wavelets yields a phasor arc sum.[cite: 2]
Total phase difference β between wavelets from top and bottom edges: β = (2π / λ) a sin(θ).[cite: 2]
Single-Slit Intensity Formula: I = I_0 [ sin(β / 2) / (β / 2) ]² = I_0 [ sin(π a sin θ / λ) / (π a sin θ / λ) ]².[cite: 2]
Most wave power (>90%) is concentrated inside the central maximum peak between the m = -1 and m = +1 minima.[cite: 2]
Secondary side maxima intensities drop rapidly: I_1 ≈ 0.047 I_0, I_2 ≈ 0.017 I_0, I_3 ≈ 0.008 I_0.[cite: 2]

notes.title: Diffraction Gratings & Envelope Modulation
content: Diffraction Grating: An array of N closely spaced parallel slits with slit separation distance d = 1 / N.[cite: 2]
Grating Principal Maxima Condition: d sin(θ) = m λ (m = 0, ±1, ±2...).[cite: 2]
Peak Intensity scaling: Principal maximum intensity scales as N² (I_max ∝ N²), while line width sharpens proportionally to 1/N.[cite: 2]
Finite Slit Width Envelope: Real double slits or gratings exhibit combined interference and diffraction: I = I_0 cos²(φ/2) [sin(β/2) / (β/2)]².[cite: 2]
Missing Orders occur when an interference maximum coincides with a single-slit diffraction minimum: m_interference / m_diffraction = d / a.[cite: 2]

notes.title: Master Exam Equations: Single vs Double Slit
content: CRITICAL DISTINCTION: 'a' is single slit aperture width; 'd' is center-to-center slit separation distance.[cite: 2]
Equation Trap: 'a sin θ = m λ' yields DARK MINIMA for single-slit diffraction.[cite: 2]
Equation Trap: 'd sin θ = m λ' yields BRIGHT MAXIMA for double slits and diffraction gratings.[cite: 2]
Maximum Observable Orders: Find m_max by setting sin(θ) ≤ 1.00: m_max = floor(d / λ) or floor(a / λ).[cite: 2]
If a slit is narrower than the wavelength (a < λ), no diffraction minima can form and only one broad central maximum spreads across the screen.[cite: 2]
